Ask your team which AI tools they used on study work this week. Then ask which of those tools are on your approved list.
  
Most sponsors I talk to can't answer the second question, because there is no list.
  
Meanwhile the work is already happening:
  
A CRA drafts a monitoring report from source documents in a consumer chatbot.
A medical writer pastes an unblinded listing into a public model to "tighten the language."
A contract data manager lets an unvalidated tool clean a dataset before it hits EDC.
  
None of these people are being reckless. They're being productive with the tools they have. Across enterprises, roughly seven in ten employees now use AI at least a few times a week, a fifth to a third do it outside IT's view, and nearly a third have had zero training from their employer. I have no reason to think clinical research is any different, and a few reasons to think the consequences are worse.
  
E6(R3) put ultimate responsibility for trial conduct on the sponsor, including computerized systems your contractors brought in the door. FDA's AI guidance expects a defined context of use and a credibility assessment for any model touching regulatory decisions. Neither of those documents cares whether the tool was sanctioned. They care whether you can show what it did to the data.
  
IT can lock down a corporate laptop. IT cannot decide whether the CRA at a site is competent to use AI with source documents on a personal device. That's a hiring, onboarding, and training decision, and right now almost no one owns it.
  
We decided to stop treating this as the sponsor's problem to solve after our people show up.
  
Every person on our bench now gets assessed on practical AI competence before they're placed: which tools are appropriate for which tasks, what may never go into a public model, how to verify and document AI-assisted work, how to spot fabricated content. Then they're trained to a common curriculum before day one, with completion tracked so a sponsor can audit it. We refresh the curriculum every quarter because the tools change that fast.
  
It's not complicated. It is work, and someone has to own it.
  
If you're building this internally, the three things that matter most: inventory what's already in use (ask, don't assume), publish an acceptable use standard and make training a condition of system access for contractors, and put AI competence on the interview scorecard for any role that touches study data.
  
The exposure isn't that your people are using AI. It's that nobody decided how.

After being laid off and getting limited traction in a job market saturated with job seekers, it’s easy to question your worth to prospective employers. Knowing that each opportunity may or may not afford you a sliver of time to capture the attention of hiring teams, the weight of the words used in your resume can either get you noticed or tossed aside by AI models pre-screening hundreds of job applications, while the weight of your world is on your shoulders to provide for your family and put food on your table.

I want to remind those in the same boat to live in that pocket of continuous improvement. Every job that catches your eye is an opportunity to understand what attracts employers, and consequently an opportunity to make your resume stand out more. Refine and iterate. And when you think you’re done, refine and iterate again.

Any time I question my worth to prospective employers, I remind myself that I have a very particular set of skills that I have acquired over my career (thank you, Liam Neeson). Skills that I’ve used to develop incredible working relationships. Skills that I’ve used to drive successful projects on time and under budget. Skills that have driven contract renewals and client confidence, ultimately improving my past employers’ bottom lines. My job is to make sure this is as accurately portrayed in my resume and job submittals as possible. And this is an ongoing effort.

So, to my fellow job seekers… don’t doubt yourself. Seek improvement while quietly and confidently knowing that while there’s a lot of employers missing out on you, the one that eventually hires you is investing in someone who’s highly motivated to succeed.

I’m with you!

🚀 The best software isn't built for requirements that never change. It's built to handle change without breaking everything around it.
In enterprise development, change is constant.
A business rule changes.
A new integration gets introduced.
Traffic increases.
Security requirements evolve.
A workflow that worked for thousands of transactions suddenly needs to support millions.
Over my 11 years as a Senior .NET Full Stack Developer, I've learned that good architecture isn't about making a system complicated enough to handle every possible future scenario.
It's about making the right decisions today so tomorrow's changes are easier to manage.
That could mean keeping APIs loosely coupled, separating business logic properly, using event-driven communication where it makes sense, designing reusable frontend components, optimizing the data layer, or building automated CI/CD pipelines so changes can reach production safely and consistently.
My experience across Airlines, Banking, Healthcare, and Government has given me the opportunity to work across the complete application lifecycle-from .NET APIs, Microservices, Angular and React to SQL Server, Kafka, Azure, AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, DevOps automation, and AI-enabled solutions.

The most important AI trend for 2026 that no one is talking about is the shift from building models to building the infrastructure that models can inhabit. The context confirms that agentic AI is coming of age, but the non-obvious lesson is that the bottleneck is no longer model capability. It is the ability to create persistent, stateful environments where agents can operate reliably over time.

This year, we are seeing a fundamental architectural transition. The early generation of AI was stateless: you asked a question, got an answer, and the context was lost. The next generation requires stateful, long-running agents that maintain context, remember past interactions, and coordinate with other agents. This is not a trivial engineering problem. It requires rethinking how we handle memory, context windows, and session management at the system level.

The teams that are winning are not the ones with the biggest models. They are the ones that have solved the problem of agent-to-agent communication with formalized contracts and bounded trust. They are building systems where agents have explicit permissions, explicit failure modes, and explicit handoff protocols. This is not about making agents smarter. It is about making them predictable and composable.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can fine-tune the latest foundation model. It is the one who can design the orchestration layer that makes multi-agent systems safe, debuggable, and scalable. I specialize in this. I build the infrastructure that lets AI operate as a reliable part of a distributed system, not as a black box.

The hardest engineering problem in AI right now is not the model. It is the environment around the model. If your organization is moving from single-copilot demos to production multi-agent systems, what is the one state management challenge you are struggling with most?

I optimize and automate businesses for a living.  But here is what businesses should NOT automate, on purpose.

- Discovery meetings; recorded them, but when people talk, the problems surface
- Sending money, refunds or approving payments.
- Signing contracts or accepting legal terms.
- Submitting regulatory or compliance filings.
- Hiring, firing or disciplinary decisions.
- Changing critical access rights or deleting important data.
- Confirming information that must be legally authoritative.
- High-stakes customer situations where context and strategy matter.

AI can do most of the work: 

Find the information. Check documents. Prepare the forms. Draft the response. Flag inconsistencies. Recommend the next action.

Then stop.

And ask a human.

Here is what nothing changing looks like in practice.

Elsie Lokken was 91 years old and recovering from a fall when an AI model recommended cutting her rehabilitation care. Her doctors appealed. The appeal overturn rate for that system ran above 80 percent. Fewer than one percent of patients ever appeal. The system was not designed to be right. It was designed to be too expensive to fight.

Derek Mobley applied for 107 jobs and received zero interviews. A University of Washington study found AI hiring models preferred white-associated names 85 percent of the time. Black male names were preferred over white male names in zero percent of tests. Derek never knew an algorithm had rejected him every single time.

Angela Lipps was babysitting her four grandchildren when US Marshals arrived at her home at gunpoint. West Fargo Police had run her photograph through a facial recognition system. The system matched her to a suspect in a bank fraud case in North Dakota, a state she had never visited. She spent five months in jail. Charges were dismissed on Christmas Eve after her attorney produced bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time. The facial recognition subscription remains active. The agency loans access to other departments on request.


In every one of these cases, the same conversation happened.

The developer said the model performed within acceptable parameters. The company said they followed the vendor's recommended implementation. The institution said the algorithm was just one input among many. The regulator said existing frameworks needed updating.
And the person who got hurt was left to navigate a system specifically structured so that nobody with the authority to fix it ever has to pay for what it does.

This is not a technology problem. It is a responsibility problem.

The executives signing the procurement contracts for these systems, the boards approving the budgets, the HR directors deploying the hiring algorithms, the hospital administrators licensing the denial models, they are not passive bystanders. They made a choice. They chose a tool. They are accountable for what that tool does.+

The fact that the tool is an algorithm does not change that. The fact that the decision happens in milliseconds does not change that. The fact that the outcome is described in the vendor's language rather than their own does not change that.

When your system gets it wrong, you pay. Not the developer. Not the model. You.

That is the argument Nobody Pays makes. Not as a theory. As a case file, with names, with numbers, with the companies' own AI systems quoted against them.

This week a bunch of AI “consultants” will lie to you. 
And you will believe them. 

They will present a magic AI wand that promises better outcomes. 
You may even buy it. 

I read a post this week saying owners don't care about AI, they care about outcomes, and AI just happens to be the best vehicle for getting them in 2026 and probably for decades.

First half's right. 
Nobody wakes up wanting AI.
Second half is where it breaks down and it’s how you know you’re dealing with someone who is cosplaying. 

The villain here is isn’t the cosplaying marketing bro. 
It’s the grift that AI will create some magical outcome by itself. 

Here are 3 scenarios where AI was sold as a magic wand and what happens when there is no system. 

 1️⃣ Summarize your morning emails.
Fine. Useful, even. Nobody's arguing.
Except it only works if somebody decided what urgent actually means around here. Otherwise you show up at 8am with one more thing to read, sorted by something that reckons a newsletter and a client threatening to walk are the same priority.

2️⃣ Fix our hiring.
Oof. 
Workday is currently defending a nationwide collective action over AI screening applicants.
The tool did exactly what it was built to do. 
That was the problem. 

3️⃣ Look at this legal matter.
Lawyers have been sanctioned for filing case law that doesn't exist. 
More than once. More than one court.
The citations looked perfect every time.

Same wand. Three rooms.

This is what the marketing bro doesn’t want to say…

Every one of those outcomes existed before any of this showed up.
Faster responses. Smoother hiring. Better contract review. 

Businesses have been doing all three for a century with a checklist, a template, a trained person and somebody who gave a damn.

So either they need AI (which is obviously nonsense) or AI is *one* way to get there.

None of this is an argument against the tool. 
I do this for a living.
It's an argument about order.

Look at the system. 
Find where the work actually breaks. 
Then, and only then, decide what goes there.

Sometimes that's AI. 
Sometimes it's a checklist. 
Sometimes it's hiring somebody.

The businesses getting real results didn't find a better wand.
They fixed the room first.

I created a 60 second quiz that will tell you how ready your business is for AI. 
Try it. 
What it won’t do is try to sell you a magic AI wand that you don’t need

I pitched my boss some bold asks before signing a new contract several weeks ago.

App development. A coaching program. A bigger presence on social media. Entrepreneurial work beyond my job title.
 
He said yes to all of it.

This isn't a brown-noser post to brag about how great my GM is — although he is. But to give affirmation to all the other TV journalists who believe there's a way to scale the businesses that is of mutual benefit to you and your company — you're not crazy. It can be done. In fact, I got my affirmation from a former TV news head honcho named Wendy McMahon.

Wendy is a highly respected former president of Disney O&Os and CBS News. She has a great newsletter called Pure Mettle. Her February edition was titled: "Your Best People are About to Leave," noting journalists have been leaving TV news because they've been forced to choose between building and monetizing their own audience or the station's.

That fork in the road isn't necessary.

Here's what Wendy said in her newsletter: 

"Find your best people... Trust them... Let them stay on your platform." But also "Let them build their own business. Their own newsletter. Their own speaking gigs and podcasts. Their own sponsors."

"Relax the exclusivity," she said.

Thank you, Wendy.

This affirmed much of what I had thought for a long time. And it gave me the confidence to put forth a plan in front of my boss, a plan that — again — he said yes to.

We both get additional reach and revenue. 

I get support for my entrepreneurship and the station continues to build its brand. 

This isn't a new idea.
 
James Spann has been the chief meteorologist at ABC 33/40 in Birmingham for nearly 30 years. He also built and runs the Alabama Weather Network, a statewide brand, which includes social media, with his station's full support. He didn't have to choose.
 
Al Roker's done the same thing for over a decade — still on Today, while running Al Roker Entertainment, a real production company.
 
In fact, Gray Media recently posted an opening for a "Digital News Influencer." And NBCUniversal trained a whole group of reporters to build for social platforms.
 
If stations are hiring people to build audience and personal brand on social platforms, the cognitive dissonance against letting existing talent do the same thing on their own time makes even less sense.

This renaissance needs to happen. We all know it's the Wild West in TV news right now. A modern strategy should have been in place yesterday.

National entry-level reporter pay still sits around $35–45K.

Local TV news employment dropped for the second straight year in 2025.

Consolidation is accelerating all of it.

And now we have to worry about AI anchors??
 
If a job can disappear that easily, the people doing it should be allowed to build something that doesn't disappear with it.
 
If I can help affirm your career strategy, in any way, hit me up.
 
Let's lift each other up. Let's be atypical.
